name: Diffuse Leptomeningeal Melanocytosis

criteria.description: Neurological symptoms consistent with diffuse leptomeningeal involvement such as seizures, hydrocephalus, or cranial nerve palsies
MRI demonstrating diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement and thickening without a discrete mass lesion
Biopsy showing proliferation of melanocytic cells within the leptomeninges without malignant features
Absence of primary cutaneous or ocular melanoma to exclude metastatic leptomeningeal melanoma

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of neurological symptoms plus characteristic MRI findings and confirmatory histopathology
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis requires exclusion of primary melanoma and other leptomeningeal diseases.

searchTerms: fits caused by brain membrane irritation
cranial nerve palsies causing facial or eye problems

common.symptomName: Headache due to increased intracranial pressure
searchTerms: head pain from increased intracranial pressure

common.symptomName: Vomiting associated with raised intracranial pressure
searchTerms: nausea due to raised intracranial pressure

occasional.symptomName: Visual disturbances due to optic nerve involvement

rare.symptomName: Endocrine dysfunction secondary to hypothalamic involvement
searchTerms: endocrine dysfunction caused by brain lesion

rare.symptomName: Cutaneous melanocytic lesions (when associated with neurocutaneous melanosis)
searchTerms: dark skin spots linked to nerve condition

laboratory: CSF analysis may show elevated protein and presence of melanocytes
imaging: MRI with diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement and thickening
genetic: Somatic mutations in NRAS or BRAF reported in some cases
other: Histopathology showing benign melanocytic proliferation without atypia or mitotic activity

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of malignant melanocytic cells with atypia and mitoses
History or evidence of primary cutaneous or ocular melanoma
Presence of large or multiple congenital melanocytic nevi on skin
Often associated with parenchymal melanosis in brain
May coexist with diffuse leptomeningeal melanocytosis but with distinct cutaneous findings

redFlags: Signs of increased intracranial pressure (severe headache, vomiting, papilledema)
New onset seizures or cranial nerve deficits
references: Kusters MA, et al. Diffuse leptomeningeal melanocytosis: clinical and pathological features. Neurology. 2015.
Kinsler VA, et al. Neurocutaneous melanosis and leptomeningeal melanocytosis: a review. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017.
Orphanet Report on Diffuse Leptomeningeal Melanocytosis, ORPHA:252031.
